# Apply a LUT

- Route: `/tools/apply-lut-to-photo`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `apply-lut-to-photo`

## Summary

Drop a .cube 3D LUT onto a photo, set its intensity and export the graded image at full resolution. (Photo editing)

## Details

A LUT is a lookup table that maps every input color to an output color, and the .cube format is how most camera profiles, film emulations and video grades are shared. Aperture accepts a .cube file as a LUT layer: the table is parsed in the browser, quantized to bytes, uploaded to the GPU as a 3D texture and sampled trilinearly for every pixel of the 1920 px preview, after whatever exposure, curves or color layers sit below it in the stack. An Intensity slider blends between the untouched pixel and the looked-up one. Because the LUT text is stored inside the project document, the export server reads the same table and applies the same interpolation to the original at full size, so a grade built for video footage lands on a 24 megapixel still exactly as intended.
### What it does
- Adds a LUT layer: drop a .cube file or choose one, and the panel reports the cube size once the table parses.
- Applies a 3D LUT of any size from 2 to 65 points per axis, up to 1 MB of text, with trilinear interpolation between the eight nearest table entries.
- Blends the looked-up color with the input through an Intensity slider from 0 to 1, so a heavy cinematic grade can be used at half strength.
- Stacks with every other adjustment: put exposure or white balance below the LUT so the table receives a normalized image, and curves or grain above it.
- Removes the table with one click and keeps the layer slot, and records the load and every intensity change in the undoable history.
### How to use it
1. Drop a photo: The editor opens on the LUT panel with the image decoded locally.
2. Load the .cube file: Drag the LUT onto the panel or choose it; the size check and the parse run in the browser.
3. Set the intensity: Slide Intensity down from 1 if the full table is too strong; use the before/after split to compare.
4. Export: Pick a format, quality and size; the server renders the original with the same table.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP, .cube (3D LUT, size 2-65, up to 1 MB)
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- The .cube table is quantized to 8 bits per entry and sampled trilinearly; 1D LUTs and tables larger than 1 MB are refused.
- Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
### Technical details
- A .cube file is plain text. A LUT_3D_SIZE N line declares the grid, optional TITLE, DOMAIN_MIN, DOMAIN_MAX and LUT_3D_INPUT_RANGE lines are skipped, comment lines start with #, and then N x N x N rows of three floats follow with red varying fastest, then green, then blue. A size-33 cube therefore has 35,937 rows and a size-65 cube has 274,625.
- The parser accepts a header from 2 up to 65; files that declare LUT_1D_SIZE are refused because only 3D tables are supported. The text is capped at 1 MB (1,048,576 bytes), and since a size-33 table with six-decimal values is already about 970 KB, 33 is the largest common grid that fits; a size-65 file would be about 7 MB and is rejected as too big before parsing.
- Every table value is quantized to a byte, round(value x 255) clamped to 0..255, so the table can be uploaded as an RGB8 3D texture. A value of 0.5 becomes 128/255 = 0.50196; this is the only precision loss and it is below the 8-bit export tolerance.
- Lookup is trilinear: the input color is scaled to 0..N-1 per axis, the lower cell index is floor(value) capped at N-2, and the result is a lerp along red, then green, then blue between the eight surrounding entries. The output is then lerp(input, lookup, intensity), so Intensity 0.6 contributes 60 percent of the table's shift.
- The graded preview is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy of the photo, and the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same table and the same trilinear formula; the two agree within a small documented tolerance of a few 8-bit levels at most, and grain is exact.
### When not to use it
Do not reach for a LUT when the problem is a per-channel brightness mapping, since the Curves panel does that with up to 16 editable points and no file to manage, or when you only want to tone shadows and highlights, which the split-toning page does with two hue sliders. A log-to-display LUT applied to an already display-referred JPEG will wreck the contrast; use the Basic panel instead. And if your table is larger than 1 MB or a 1D LUT, it must be converted elsewhere first.
### Use cases
- Match stills to graded footage: Apply the same .cube used on a video project to the behind-the-scenes photos so thumbnails and stills share the grade.
- Film emulation packs: Load a purchased or free emulation LUT and set Intensity to 0.6 for a subtler version than the full table.
- Camera profile conversions: Use a manufacturer-provided display LUT on a flat, low-contrast export from a camera's neutral profile.
- Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
### FAQ
Q: What is a .cube file?
A: A text file in the Adobe Cube format: a LUT_3D_SIZE line giving the grid size N, then N cubed lines of three output values between 0 and 1, ordered with red changing fastest. Each line is the output color for one input color on the grid; colors between grid points are interpolated.
Q: What LUT sizes and file sizes are accepted?
A: A LUT_3D_SIZE from 2 to 65 and a file no larger than 1 MB. In practice the 1 MB cap means a size-33 cube (35,937 rows) is the largest common grid that loads; size 17 (about 130 KB) and size 25 load with room to spare.
Q: Why does a 1D LUT fail to load?
A: Only 3D tables are supported. A file that declares LUT_1D_SIZE is refused with the invalid-file message; convert it to a 3D cube in the tool that made it, or rebuild the per-channel transform with the Curves panel, which does the same job for 1D tables.
Q: Does the LUT expect a log or a normal image?
A: That depends on the LUT. Camera log-to-display tables expect flat log footage, and applying one to a normal JPEG crushes contrast. Look-style tables made for display images are the right kind for ordinary photos. The Intensity slider will not fix a wrong-input-space LUT.
Q: Are the colors interpolated or snapped to the grid?
A: Interpolated. Each channel of the output is a trilinear blend of the eight grid entries around the input color, so a size-17 table still produces smooth gradients rather than visible steps.
Q: Is the LUT sent to a third party?
A: No. The table is kept in the project document, parsed in the browser and read by our own export server; nothing about the file or the photo is shared with anyone else.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Use when someone has a .cube 3D LUT (a colour grade or film look) and wants to apply it to a photo at a chosen intensity and export at full resolution. Typical asks: "apply my LUT to this image".
When to send them elsewhere: Without a LUT file, use Curves (photo-curves) for tone mapping or Split toning (split-toning) for shadow and highlight hues. 1D LUTs and very large tables are not supported. A log-to-display LUT on a normal JPEG will look wrong.
Related tools: photo-curves (hand-built tone mapping); split-toning (simple two-hue grade); tint-photo (single-colour wash); fix-photo-exposure (correct exposure before grading)
